chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, and Safwan ibn Yahya, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When you have finished your Tawaf and reached the rear of the Kaaba, which is opposite Al-Mustajar, slightly before the Yamani Corner, then spread your hands towards the House, press your belly and cheek against the House, and say: 'O Allah, the House is Your House, and the servant is Your servant, and this is the place of the one seeking refuge with You from the Fire.'
Then acknowledge to your Lord for what you have done, for there is no believing servant who acknowledges to his Lord his sins in this place except that Allah will forgive him, if Allah wills.

And you should say: 'O Allah, from You is the comfort, the relief, and the health. O Allah, my deeds are weak, so multiply them for me, and forgive me what You have taken notice of from me, which was concealed from Your creatures.'
Then seek refuge with Allah from the Fire, and choose for yourself from the supplications, then touch the Yamani Corner, then go to the Black Stone.

key_terms.اسْتَلَمَ: To touch/kiss the stone with the hand and kiss the hand
key_terms.الْمُسْتَجَارِ: Al-Mustajar (the section of the wall opposite the door)
key_terms.الْمُلْتَزَم: Al-Multazam (the place of embracing/pressing against the wall)
key_terms.مُؤَخَّرَ الْكَعْبَةِ: The rear/back part of the Kaaba

ai.seo_question: What is the supplication and ritual procedure for Al-Multazam during Hajj or Umrah?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi details the specific ritual of Al-Multazam, where the pilgrim presses their chest and cheeks against the Kaaba's wall to emulate the Prophet's practice and seek divine mercy. It emphasizes the theological concept of *istighatha* (seeking refuge) and the efficacy of sincere confession (*iqrar*) of sins in this sacred spot, a practice highly regarded in Shia jurisprudence for expiation. The supplication highlights the contrast between human weakness and God's boundless grace, reinforcing the pilgrim's status as a dependent servant seeking protection from the Fire.
